video_title: What It Takes to Build an AI That Actually Knows You
gist: Ken, founder of First Person Labs, makes his first public appearance on a16z to describe 'second', an always-on personal user model built from the OS activity stream and connectors that other agents (Grockbot, Codex) query as portable context. Key investor takeaways: confidential (attested GPU) inference displacing zero-data-retention promises, ~$1,000/day Opus vs ~$60/day cheap-model costs for ambient agents, and a mixture-of-models harness as token prices fall.

themes.theme: Personal user model as portable context layer for agents

insights.claim: First Person Labs is building 'second', a persistent model of a person (memories, priorities, preferences, goals, values, commitments, intent) that other agents such as Grockbot or Codex query as portable context instead of re-asking the user.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: A new 'personal context' layer is forming between users and agent apps; watch who owns the user model as a potential control point.
insights.quote: we focus on essentially creating a model of a person and then put that person in control

insights.claim: Ken argues having many personal agents is transitory: agents will specialize (e.g., shopping agents with data and connections), while one trusted agent per person holds life context like a vault and spins up ephemeral sub-agents.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Implies winner-take-most dynamics for the trusted personal-data agent slot; specialized vertical agents become clients of it.
insights.quote: the fact that we have many personal agents is probably transitory like agents will start to specialize just like people do

insights.claim: A host says portable context let him switch to a newly released OpenAI cyber-capable model in Codex without losing prior work context, lowering switching costs between frontier tools.
insights.speaker: a16z host
insights.so_what: Portable user context erodes lock-in for model/agent vendors and makes switching to the newest model nearly free.

insights.claim: Ken claims the biggest bottleneck in AI assistants today is that users have to ask; the goal is agents that intervene and act for the user without prompting.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Shift from prompt-driven to proactive/ambient AI changes product design and inference demand (always-on background compute).
insights.quote: one of the biggest bottness right now like people have to ask

themes.theme: Ambient OS event stream as untapped data source

insights.claim: Operating systems (Apple, Microsoft, Linux) already expose an endless stream of events—app switches, typing, browsing pauses, Wi-Fi—and First Person Labs runs 24/7 agents that hierarchically synthesize this into an understanding of what the user is doing, supplemented by connectors (Slack, Signal, WhatsApp).
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: The raw computer-activity stream is an underexploited data asset; connectors improve sample efficiency but are not the core.
insights.quote: people are very underestimating like how much the computer already knows

insights.claim: Ken distinguishes reactive productivity (responding to a new email) from reflective productivity (connecting dots across months of events, goals and to-dos), arguing the latter is harder and far more valuable.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Differentiation in personal AI will come from long-horizon reasoning over context, not notification triage.

insights.claim: Early users (a16z hosts) report the product proactively surfaced relevant information unprompted, e.g., continuously updating an event's weather forecast to decide whether to rent a tent.
insights.speaker: a16z host
insights.so_what: Early-adopter evidence of proactive value; a16z partners are vocal power users, signalling investor backing.

insights.claim: Ken says the product exposes the user as APIs (what you did 10 minutes ago, next week's priorities, reminders, a wiki of people in your life), and expects third-party and personal apps to be built on top—likening it to the Altair 8800 awaiting its spreadsheet killer app.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: A 'personal infra' platform play; the killer app is not yet found, so value accrues to whoever builds on the context API.

themes.theme: Confidential inference vs zero data retention

insights.claim: Ken says AI reduces to data plus inference, so second lets users bring their own tokens to analyze data kept locally, or use a provider running models inside confidential-computing GPUs where the trust anchor is Nvidia hardware.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Confidential computing on GPUs becomes a requirement for personal-data AI workloads—supportive for Nvidia's confidential-computing features and attestation-capable providers.
insights.quote: the hardware is what you trust, which is Nvidia

insights.claim: Zero data retention is only a policy promise ('I give you my word'), whereas confidential inference is technically provable via hardware attestation; Ken expects confidential inference to become the default for personal data.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Watch for inference providers adding attestable confidential inference; ZDR-only providers may lose personal-data workloads.
insights.quote: Zero data retention is a promise by policy

insights.claim: Ken notes third-party inference providers are ramping confidential inference and believes OpenAI announced such an option within the last month, because all personal data will want to go to confidential rather than standard inference.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Signals confidential inference moving into mainstream frontier-lab offerings.

insights.claim: Storage follows password-manager/iCloud patterns: a local-only mode, or cloud backup encrypted locally and decrypted only inside an attested confidential container, completing an end-to-end trust chain.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Security architecture borrowed from password managers is the adoption unlock for always-on personal AI.

insights.claim: Ken concedes LLM-level data-sharing guarantees (e.g., resisting prompt-injection tricks) cannot be definitively solved; deterministic rules handle hard cases while reasoning-based guarantees improve as model capability scales.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent data leakage remains an open risk for personal-agent products; security is capability-bound.

insights.claim: Ken estimates running 10 always-on agents at 60 tokens/second at Opus pricing costs about $1,000 per day, versus about $60 per day with a DeepSeek Flash-class model, so the product initially targets busy professionals.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Ambient agents are massive token consumers; falling inference prices directly expand the addressable market and inference demand.
insights.quote: at Opus 5i's pricing that leads to $1,000 per day

insights.claim: Ken says token prices have already dropped more than 50% since the company started, and expects costs to keep falling quickly as new models are swapped in.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Continued inference deflation is a tailwind for always-on agent apps and a margin pressure on model vendors.
insights.quote: token prices already dropped like by more than 50%

insights.claim: Cost/fidelity trade-off is framed as 'cache time' (continuously pre-analyzing data into deeper insights, expensive) versus test time (reasoning over raw logs on demand, roughly 10x slower).
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for evaluating personal-AI unit economics.

insights.claim: Second is a harness-design problem: cheap models detect semantically meaningful events frequently, expensive frontier models infer weekly goals infrequently, and specialist models (e.g., one Ken calls 'Jeff') excel at retrieval—so the system becomes a mixture of models for cost efficiency, and open-weight models are 'pretty smart these days'.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Model-agnostic harnesses commoditize individual model providers; routing layer captures value.

insights.claim: After mistakes going all-in on interaction design, First Person Labs closed down surfaces to texting and an API (usable as a cloud MCP), leaving UI and applications to others while it focuses on systems and understanding.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Positions the company as infrastructure rather than consumer app; distribution depends on agent ecosystems like Grockbot.

insights.claim: Ken envisions a long-run world where everyone has a second and all devices become inputs and outputs (screens, doorbell, orbs), achieving the ubiquity of Jarvis that today's closest analogue, Apple iCloud sync, lacks for AI; current OS lockdown (e.g., iPad) limits this.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Platform owners (Apple) control access to ambient context; OS-level restrictions are a key risk for third-party personal AI.

insights.claim: The product is available today but rollout is gated by scaling inference capacity, per Ken.
insights.speaker: Ken (founder, First Person Labs)
insights.so_what: Inference capacity constraints even for startups underline continued compute demand.
